preamble: A coda /t/ takes on the bilabial place of a following /p/, /b/ or /m/, giving [p] (regressive place assimilation). The process is asymmetric: coronals assimilate to labials and velars, while labials and velars rarely assimilate to coronals. In English and German connected speech it is variable and frequency-dependent, and corpus and perception studies document complete assimilations (sit politely heard as sip politely; German bunt machen [bʊmp]). Korean shows the same process at the coda–onset boundary in fast speech, which the Standard Pronunciation rules exclude from the standard. In Sino-Japanese compounds the original coda /t/ of borrowed Middle Chinese morphemes became fully assimilated to a following /p/, giving geminate [pp] as in shuppatsu and shippai.

examples.note: Gaskell and Snoeren (2008) use this example of how place assimilation can make sit sound like sip; their production data show that complete assimilations occur in casual speech.

Example cited by Zimmerer, Reetz and Lahiri (2009) from Kohler; in their Kiel corpus of conversational German, 4 of 200 /t/-final function words were transcribed with [p] before a labial, and none assimilated to a dorsal.

The coda /t/ (neutralized from ㅊ) assimilates to the following bilabial /p/. Standard Pronunciation Article 21 rejects this form as non-standard but notes that it occurs in rapid speech (also 문법 [문뻡], *[뭄뻡] 'grammar' for n > m).

Coda /t/ of a Sino-Japanese morpheme (from Middle Chinese -t) does not take its epenthetic vowel before a voiceless obstruent and is realized as the geminate mora /Q/, copying the place of the following /p/.
Same assimilation; 一 ichi + 杯 hai gives 一杯 ippai 'one cup, full'.
